headline: Comparing the Two Cities

elements.note: Stays black (#111112). One line now.
Second headline line no longer needed.
Local Law 97 covers buildings over 25,000 sq ft. Shorter than the old text, so it fits.

movedToNotes: Both cities have the same problem with their buildings. Seoul helps owners pay for upgrades with cheap loans, and New York fines owners whose buildings go over a carbon limit.
Both cities are very dense and build tall. Seoul is mostly apartments, and New York has a mix of building types. Neither city has free land for new parks.
Population numbers are rounded.
New York's buildings share changes from year to year in its emissions inventories, so the slide shows a range (66 to 71%). Seoul's 67% comes from its current climate plan.
Seoul: Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth
Seoul's Building Retrofit Program (BRP, since 2008): loans up to 100% of the eligible cost at 1.75% a year
New York: Local Law 97 (2019), buildings over 25,000 sq ft
LL97 fine: $268 for every ton of CO₂e over the building's limit
Next: why buildings? Show the split.

movedToNotes: About two-thirds of Seoul's emissions come from buildings that are already standing, so most of the work is fixing existing buildings.
Sources disagree on the exact buildings share: 67% (current plan), 68.2% (Seoul's 2020 Green New Deal release), 68.8% (UNESCAP, 2018 data). Say "roughly two-thirds".

Transportation 18%: the plan says buildings plus transport make 85%, and 85 minus 67 is 18. If someone asks about the other 15%: I only have the buildings and transport numbers, so I can't break down the rest.

52.34 Mt CO₂e = Seoul's total emissions in 2005 (Mt = million tons). The 2033 goal is to cut that in half. The 2050 goal is carbon neutrality (net zero). CO₂e = all greenhouse gases counted as the amount of CO₂ that would have the same warming effect.
Baseline year = the starting year Seoul measures its cuts against (2005).
Point to the red area on the map: that's Seoul.

movedToNotes: Two problems pushed Seoul to act: first the Nanjido landfill, then Fukushima and the Seoul blackout in 2011, which led to One Less Nuclear Power Plant.
1977 to 1978: Nanjido, an island in the Han River, is joined to the mainland and becomes the city dump. It was easy to reach and far from downtown.
Two mounds about 90 m high. Korea had no modern treatment yet for the gas or the dirty liquid draining out of the trash, so methane and toxic gases leaked.
1993: the city decides to close the dump (some sources say dumping ended in 1992). 2002: it opens as World Cup Park. More on Nanjido on slide 14.
2011: Fukushima, then a blackout in Seoul the same year
Background today: Korea makes only about a fifth of its own energy (22.1% in 2024, 35th of 38 OECD countries)
OECD = a group of 38 mostly wealthy countries
Next: the plan that came out of this, with real target dates.
